analysis.one_liner: Spends at least $1 trillion a year for a decade on jobs, clean energy, housing, and care work.
analysis.headline: A $1-trillion-a-year jobs and climate bill with 66 House Democratic cosponsors never got a hearing or a vote in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The THRIVE Act would have set up a ten-year federal investment program, authorizing at least $1 trillion per year from 2022 through 2032, aimed at creating at least 15.5 million jobs. The money would have funded clean energy and transit, building retrofits, housing, care work, pollution cleanup, and manufacturing, with strings attached: union rights, a $15-or-prevailing-wage floor, paid leave, and a requirement that at least half the money go to low-income and pollution-burdened communities. It prohibited new fossil fuel extraction and penalties for companies with histories of concentrated pollution. It was referred to six House committees, none of which acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the primary beneficiaries would have been low-income workers and communities facing pollution and economic disinvestment: the bill required at least half of all funding to go to those communities, guaranteed jobs paying at least $15 an hour or the prevailing wage with paid leave, and prioritized hiring from groups facing employment barriers. Workers in construction, care work, manufacturing, and clean energy would have seen a large customer in the federal government with union and wage conditions attached. Tribes and Indigenous communities would have received dedicated funding and consent requirements for projects affecting their land.

how_it_helps.text: Authorized appropriations of 'not less than $1,000,000,000,000' for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2032 and set a target of creating and supporting at least 15,500,000 family-sustaining jobs.
Required that at least 50 percent of total funding be invested in low-income and pollution-burdened communities, with mandatory equity assessments to prevent further concentration of pollution.

Required funded projects to provide wages of at least $15 an hour or the prevailing wage, at least 84 days of paid family leave, 14 days of paid sick leave, and the right to organize and bargain collectively free of employer interference.

Set firm transition targets, including 100 percent zero-emission new construction by the end of 2025, 100 percent clean electricity generation by 2035, and conversion of all school buses in operation by 2035 to zero-emission models.

Directed funding to care workers — domestic workers, health care workers, home health aides — including wage and benefit increases for historically underpaid care work, and to remediation of Superfund, brownfield, and abandoned fossil fuel sites.

Required free, prior, and informed consent of Tribal nations for agency actions affecting Tribal land, water, and culture, and mandated a set-aside of investments for Tribes and Indigenous communities.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on federal taxpayers, at a scale of at least $10 trillion over the decade. Fossil fuel producers would have lost the ability to expand extraction and faced new penalties and liabilities for historic pollution, with the bill explicitly barring those costs from being passed to ratepayers or consumers. Private companies competing for the funding would have had to accept union-friendly conditions, prevailing wages, and domestic content requirements. Entities that privatize public infrastructure or use emissions offsets would have been excluded from funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: The mandatory funding floor of at least $1 trillion per year for fiscal years 2022 through 2032 would have added roughly $10 trillion in authorized spending over a decade, far larger than any infrastructure or climate bill that Congress actually considered.

Several targets were aggressive to the point of likely infeasibility, such as requiring 100 percent of newly constructed buildings nationwide to be zero-emission by the end of 2025, less than five years after introduction.

The President and a 20-member advisory board would have gained sweeping discretion to certify, condition, and revoke funding for federal programs, an unusual concentration of spending authority in the executive branch with only advisory oversight and annual reports to Congress.

Extensive labor, equity, and environmental conditions — including hiring preferences at twice industry-standard rates and interest arbitration for first contracts — would have raised compliance costs and could have slowed project delivery, an objection honest supporters had to weigh against the wage and organizing protections those same conditions created.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered an unusually direct bargain: roughly $10 trillion in public investment, most of it steered by statutory formula toward low-income communities and union-wage jobs, in exchange for a comparable cost to taxpayers and real constraints on fossil fuel expansion and low-road employers. The tradeoff was honest — the price tag was enormous and the timelines ambitious — but the distribution of benefits was written into the bill rather than left to agencies. The main design weakness was the breadth of discretionary power given to the President and an advisory board to decide which programs qualified.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees at introduction; none of them held a hearing or reported it out, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Debbie Dingell introduced the THRIVE Act on April 30, 2021, with 44 original cosponsors, and 66 House Democrats eventually signed on; no Republican cosponsored it.

The bill was referred to the Committees on Education and Labor, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Agriculture, and three subcommittees received referrals on May 3, 2021; the action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action at any point afterward.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill having received no vote in either chamber.

During the same period, Congress instead enacted a narrower bipartisan infrastructure law, showing that leadership chose a different vehicle for infrastructure spending while the THRIVE Act sat without committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and opponents of trillion-dollar public spending came out ahead, since the bill never advanced and nothing constrained them; Congress instead passed a smaller bipartisan infrastructure package in late 2021.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and spending opponents

for.name: Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 44 original cosponsors from the House Democratic caucus.

for.name: 66 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the more broadly supported progressive bills of the Congress among House Democrats.

against.name: Chairs of six House committees
against.role: Education and Labor, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearings, no markup, no report to the floor — across the full two-year Congress.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor and pursued a narrower bipartisan infrastructure package instead, which became law in November 2021.

sides.party_line_note: All 66 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill barred federal programs from expanding extraction, processing, or use of fossil fuels, and established penalties and liabilities for historic concentrated pollution in environmental justice communities, with those costs barred from passing to ratepayers or consumers. Producers had a direct financial interest in the bill never moving.

The bill required expansion of renewable energy and manufacturing of clean technologies, with domestic content standards attached, making the federal government a decade-long customer. The public benefit (clean power, jobs) and industry benefit (contracts) ran in the same direction, though with wage and domestic-production strings.

Building retrofits, transit, housing modernization, and zero-emission construction targets would have generated years of contracted work, conditioned on prevailing wages, project labor agreements, and union access.

The bill directed investment into child care, home care, elder care, and public health infrastructure, with wage and benefit increases for historically underpaid care workers — a benefit to both the workers and the providers, contingent on meeting the labor standards.

The bill prohibited privatization of public infrastructure, services, land, water, or natural resources, and directed support instead to community-owned and publicly owned utilities and cooperatives. Private investors seeking to own or operate public assets were shut out.

Contractors would have gained access to an enormous funding stream, but only by accepting union-friendly conditions, wage floors, domestic content rules, and revocation of funding for violations — a genuine trade of market access for constraints.
